summary: Provides technical specifications and linguistic guidelines for using Arabic in Internet domain names. It addresses Arabic-specific issues in the language. It is informational and not a Standards Track specification.

eli5.summary: Domain names written in Arabic need special care since the script has many forms and quirks. This note offers guidelines on how to handle them.

questions: how are arabic internationalized domain names handled
why no diacritics in domain names
subtitle: Technical rules and linguistic guidance for registering domain names in Arabic.

tldr.problem: Arabic script has unique linguistic features (diacritics, letter variations, numerals) that need careful handling in domain names to avoid confusion and preserve spelling correctness.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies which Arabic Unicode characters are allowed in domain names, prohibits problematic features like diacritics and character folding, requires numeral homogeneity, and permits hyphens as word separators.
tldr.outcome: Arabic-speaking communities can register domain names that are linguistically correct, user-friendly, and unambiguous while conforming to internationalized domain name standards.

facts.label: Numeral sets
facts.value: Western (0-9) or Arabic-Indic (0-9 in Arabic form), not mixed

facts.label: Diacritics permitted
facts.value: None; Tashkeel and Shadda are disallowed

today: RFC 5564 is an Informational RFC that codified guidelines developed by the Arab Working Group on Arabic Domain Names. The IETF and regional Internet registries (RIRs) use these guidelines to validate Arabic domain name registrations. Arabic domain names are now widely deployed in the .Middle East and Arab country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs).

sections.title: Arabic Characters on the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force defined Internationalized Domain Names (IDN) in RFC 3490 to enable domain names in non-Latin scripts. The IETF later issued IDNA2008, a revised standard that is more flexible and linguistically aware. However, IDN allows many Unicode characters, and not all are appropriate for Arabic domain names due to the linguistic properties of the Arabic script.

This RFC, developed by the Arab Working Group on Arabic Domain Names (AWG-ADN) with support from the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (UN-ESCWA), provides technical specifications and linguistic guidelines for Arabic domain names. It defines exactly which Arabic characters are permitted, which problematic features must be prohibited, and how to handle special cases like numerals and word separators all while maintaining compliance with modern IDNA standards.
sections.eli5: The Internet now lets you write addresses in any language. But Arabic has quirks that need special care to work well online.

sections.title: Arabic Linguistic Challenges
sections.content:
Arabic script presents several linguistic challenges for domain names. Diacritics (called Tashkeel) are small marks placed above or below letters to indicate vowels and pronunciation. Shadda marks consonant doubling. These marks are essential for correct reading in printed Arabic but are not suitable for domain names: they clutter the address, reduce usability, and are not needed for machine processing. IDNA2008 permits them, but this RFC recommends disallowing them in domain names.

Kasheeda (also called Tatweel) is a character used to extend the visual length of letters for graphical presentation. It serves no pronunciation or semantic purpose and adds nothing to domain names, so it is prohibited. Character folding, which means replacing similar-looking letters with a single canonical form, is also prohibited because it changes word meaning. For example, folding different forms of Hamzah or Alef into one shape would create ambiguity: one domain name would represent multiple different Arabic words, masking others.
sections.eli5: Arabic has special accent marks for pronunciation, decorative stretches for writing style, and similar-looking letters. These are fine for books but confusing in web addresses.

sections.title: Supported Character Set
sections.content:
This RFC specifies exactly which Unicode characters are allowed in Arabic domain names, using an inclusion-based approach: only listed characters are permitted. The allowed set consists of 28 base Arabic letters (from Unicode U+0621 through U+064A), 10 Arabic-Indic numerals (U+0660 through U+0669 for 0–9), and 10 Western numerals (U+0030 through U+0039). The full stop (U+002E) separates domain labels, and the hyphen-minus (U+002D) can separate words within a label.

Notably absent are diacritics, Kasheeda, and other variant forms. All other Unicode characters are prohibited. This focused set balances linguistic correctness with simplicity and unambiguity. A domain name label is a valid sequence of these characters, beginning and ending with a letter, and not using more than one numeral set in the same label.
sections.eli5: Only 28 letters, maybe some numbers, hyphens, and dots are allowed. No accent marks, no decorations, no other symbols.

sections.title: Special Rules and Constraints
sections.content:
Several special rules govern Arabic domain names. The first is numeral homogeneity: a label cannot mix Western digits (0–9) with Arabic-Indic digits (0–9 in Arabic form). This prevents confusion when typing and reading. If a label contains any digit from one set, all digits must be from that set. Both sets are supported for user interfaces and input methods, but within a single label, they must be homogeneous.

The second rule concerns space characters. Spaces are forbidden in domain names (a control character restriction). Instead, the hyphen-minus (U+002D) is used as a word separator within a label, analogous to the Arabic Al-sharta. This allows readable domain names like some-word-here without introducing spaces.

These rules aim to simplify domain names for end users while preserving Arabic linguistic correctness. They avoid the confusion that can arise from multiple numeral sets, ensure hyphens behave consistently with how Arabic-speaking users might expect separators, and eliminate characters that add no value or create ambiguity.
sections.eli5: Do not mix Western and Arabic numbers in one label. Use hyphens instead of spaces. That is it.

sections.title: Harmony with International Standards
sections.content:
This RFC is designed to be fully compliant with IDNA2008 and the IETF IDN standards (RFC 3490, RFC 3491, RFC 3492). The guidelines do not conflict with the broader internationalization framework; instead, they apply it specifically to Arabic, taking into account Arabic-language-specific issues that IDNA alone cannot address.

The recommendations were developed through intensive consultations among the Arab-speaking community, standardization experts, and Internet technologists. The goal was to reach consensus on a character set and rules that serve Arabic speakers while respecting linguistic principles. The document also notes that while it focuses on customer Ethernet-level Arabic domain names, nothing prevents TRILL solutions from being applied to provider-level services or other domains.
sections.eli5: These rules fit within the international domain name system and were agreed on by Arabic experts and Internet organizations.
